links.outcome: Readability (Gulpease) and professional ratings of consent forms: human standard vs ChatGPT-rewritten vs fully ChatGPT-generated
links.effect: Gulpease: A 36, B 66, C 82 (C most readable). Professionals rated A and C highest; B lowest (overall median 3.0 A and C vs 2.0 B); A vs C not significantly different.
links.quote: Using the Gulpease Index, the scores obtained for each consent form were: 36 for consent form A, namely incomprehensible for elementary level, very difficult for middle and high school levels.

links.outcome: Reading ease of vaccination consent form after ChatGPT rewrite
links.effect: Standard form Gulpease 36 (high complexity); ChatGPT-modified form C scored 82 (very easy for higher education, easy for general population) with comprehensibility rated similar to the standard form.
links.quote: Consent form A and consent form C obtained the highest scores in terms of adequacy, comprehensibility, completeness and overall judgement ( table 2 , figure 1 ).

links.outcome: Quality of fully AI-generated vs human-supervised AI-modified consent forms rated by professionals
links.effect: Fully ChatGPT-generated form B scored significantly lower than A and C (adequacy p<0.001 vs A; overall judgement A vs B p=0.009, B vs C p=0.002), suggesting human input is needed.
links.quote: Consent form B, generated entirely by ChatGPT, scored lower, suggesting that collaboration between AI and humans yields better results: ChatGPT alone might not be sufficient to produce the best and most accepted product, and that the best results are achieved through the collaborative use of LLMs and human expertise.

unlisted_practices: Using LLMs to simplify informed consent forms with human expert supervision

links.effect: C (ChatGPT rephrasing A) vs B (AI-only): adequacy median 4.0 vs 3.0; overall judgement 3.0 vs 2.0; B-C differences p<0.01 and p=0.002.
links.quote: Consent form B, generated entirely by ChatGPT, scored lower, suggesting that collaboration between AI and humans yields better results: ChatGPT alone might not be sufficient to produce the best and most accepted product, and that the best results are achieved through the collaborative use of LLMs and human expertise.

links.effect: Gulpease: A 36, B 66, C 82, D 63; C was easy for the general population and very easy for higher education levels.
links.quote: First, the Gulpease index, used to support the selection of consent forms to be administered to healthcare professionals, revealed that consent form C scored the highest, being the most readable.

links.effect: Comprehensibility medians: A 4.0, B 3.0, C 3.5; Kruskal-Wallis p=0.01374; A vs C p=0.26, B vs C p=0.15.
links.quote: For comprehensibility, consent form A had a median of 4.0 (IQR 3.0–4.0), consent form B a median of 3.0 (IQR 3.0–4.0) and consent form C a median of 3.5 (IQR 3.0–4.0).

links.effect: D had Gulpease 63 but was excluded as excessively colloquial.
links.quote: Although consent form D received a score of 63, which is equivalent to easy reading for the population with a middle school degree and above, it was discarded because it contained an excessively colloquial tone.

unlisted_practices: Use LLMs only as a human-supervised aid for drafting or rephrasing vaccination informed consent forms.

links.outcome: consent form adequacy, completeness, and overall judgement
links.effect: Grounded Form C significantly outperformed ungrounded Form B in adequacy (p<0.01), completeness (p=0.017), and overall judgement (p=0.002), matching standard Form A.
links.quote: Regarding the overall judgement, the analyses revealed significant differences between consent forms A and B (p=0.009), and between consent forms B and C (p=0.002), while no significant differences were found between consent forms A and C (p=0.896).

unlisted_practices: Using large language models to simplify and improve the readability of patient informed consent forms
